Shakespeare for the Homeless

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
In between taxis, and hawkers and piles of rubbish, squeezed in between decaying buildings, there’s a sign – easy to miss- that announces the Hillbrow Theatre…then down the stairs you go until to the basement and here amongst the broken chairs… England’s most famous playwright; William Shakespeare’s words are being given new life and meaning.

Around 15 men of various ages are sitting in a semi- circle. Playing to this audience is 31 year old Michael Mazibuko. He’s reciting Hamlet’s soliloquy ‘ To Be or Not To Be’. Director, Michael Maxwell is giving Mazibuko voice direction and explaining the meanings of some of these very olde English words – while he is doing this you could hear a pin drop, everyone’s attention is focused on Michaels every word.

Called Johannesburg Awakening ( Jam), this is brain child of Dorothy Anne Gould, one of South Africa’s most celebrated and respected actresses, Dorothy has starred in over 180 productions and been awarded several of South Africa’s top accolades. Dorothy’s own life was changed as teenager when she discovered the power of the spoken word.

"I fell in love with the stories and poetry of a man called William Shakespeare. These made a profound shift in my immature consciousness to a more spiritual level of understanding of my world and of humanity; they made me aware that performance in a story is a sacred art and can transform both performer and audience and that this is achieved through the use of breath, through the power of the spoken word and through the act of sublimating ones ego and playing instead, for the gods. They gave me a purpose in my life which has never wavered – uplift and serve ones’ fellow human beings through the power and magic of poetry."



Further information:
It was this she wanted to pass on and hopefully transform other lives.
She started Jam in 2012 with seven men and one woman recruited from a church soup kitchen. Some had been on the streets since they were children. With weekly classes, teaching Shakespeare and poetry and classes in acting and voice the group has grown and many have managed to improve their lives and gain employment. They range in age from 18 – 56 years old.

The classes have gradually seen men like Michael Mazibuko or Bongani Dlamini find their voice, their self respect and ambition.
Dorothy “When you have never had a voice it takes time and courage to find it…...
When your spoken voice is put out in the world then the power and images of the words start to flow through and that to some measure heals your pain.”

Shakespeare was a tough place to start but Dorothy did it also for the shock tactic: ‘ If you can recite Hamlets soliloquy at the traffic lights you will probably get some money because people don’t expect that so its breaking assumptions.
“The men challenge my assumptions too with their eloquence, enthusiasm and skills.”

They meet every Monday… now not only learning but finding their own voice in prose or poetry telling their truth’s.

Formerly homeless, Scott Edmn, has been with the group since the beginning, Scott makes the sandwiches and tea which are donated St Georges Church , and very welcome. Scott also keeps an order in the proceedings…
Michael Mazibuko says he has found his soul in Hamlet’s To Be or Not to Be “it speaks directly to me about the challenges I face every day” It also helped him learn English when Mama D (as the call Dorothy) asked him to help her translate some pieces to iZulu; Last month he played a part in soapie ‘Generations’ and was paid. Some of the others have also played roles in films and soaps.

Iwasi Mayeki, in rehearsal for Shakespeare’s Richard III, starts his soliloquy, when he reaches the line “ dogs bark at me as I halt by them,” you know he knows exactly what that feels like. Because Iwasi, has been homeless for most of his life.
Shakespeare’s words relate directly to them and reflect their own circumstances says Myeki…he was one of the original crew and joined out of curiosity. Myeke was a homeless drug user and credits Jam for turning his life around. ‘I found a place where `I can talk and my voice can be heard. It gave me something to believe in. Now I am an actor and before I was just another kid on the streets. The stories Shakespeare tells are still relevant today because it’s not just about events. It’s about people and the human condition. It talks about love and tragedy and things that are happening in our lives. Some characters have lost everything so we can connect to what he writes about. We are the perfect people to tell his stories because we have been through a lot.’

Last year Dorothy was awarded a Naledi ( the South African equivalent of the Oscars)for this innovation in theatre. The group have grown to 20 and their determination under her guidance has helped many improve their circumstance. The lessons are free and when they perform in public they keep their earnings. Most now have roofs over their heads and one sponsor pays for three of them to share a flat in Hillbrow.

This is my home, 29 year old Bongani Dlamini’s says and with a touch of drama he adds, it kept him alive. ‘ If it wasn’t for Shakespeare I wouldn’t have even gone to rehab. I was giving up because I had nothing to do and no money, I was using being an orphan as an excuse and having a lot of resentment. I always had a lot of excuses’ Shakespeare’s characters give him hope and strength because the tribulations they are experiencing are nothing new ‘
.
But its not all rainbow’s and roses Jam has seen setbacks and sadness. too with one actor going back to drugs after appearing in adverts and one relapsing after earning a place in a drama school. Four have died - two murdered one from a drug related heart attack and one from pneumonia. One was Charles who died after writing a beautiful piece saying ‘ Now I can hold up my head high’

On the 14th April the group will perform in Melville which would be good to film as part of the story… To tell the actors story through their interviews, in their words that are now being listened to. What Dorothy has done is what she knows how to do and the creative process touches and transforms both the actor and the director

Teaching Shakespeare at our South African schools has come under some controversy, but during freedom fighter, Sonny Venkatrathnam’s, incarceration on Robben Island, he smuggled in a copy of ‘The Complete Works of William Shakespeare’ disguised as a bible. This was passed between a number of prisoners including Nelson Mandela…Mandela’s signature was found next to a quote from Julius Caesar ‘ Cowards die many times before their deaths , the valiant never taste death but once’.

In April and May the 9th Shakespeare schools Festival kicks off and it will be dedicated to Sonny Venkatrathnam.

Press Release:


Shakespeare in Hillbrow
In a small dusty basement under the Hillbrow Theatre and with little more than the clothes they own, men who were all once homeless and destitute gather to recite the words of one of England’s most famous playwrights – William Shakespeare. The brainchild of celebrated South African actress Dorothy Anne Gould, “Johannesburg Awakening Minds” has been giving the men a new home in the world of the performing arts, allowing theatre to transform their lives.
Producer: Diana Lucas
Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


Shakespeare for Homeless

Link Hillbrow Theatre on Kapitein Street stands maybe not as proudly as it used to but its down stairs in their basement where magic is playing out.

Sipho: “ He hath disgraced me and hindered me half a million, laughed at my losses, mocked at my gain, hated my enemies and what is his reason? I am a homeless man,

V/O
Called Johannesburg Awakening Minds or Jam for short, this theatre group is the product of Dorothy Ann Gould, one of South Africa’s most celebrated actors. Making up Jam are people who have found themselves destitute, often homeless, living on the fringes of society.

Dorothy Ann Gould
Dorothy: I wanted them to be able to stand tall and I wanted them to be able to speak well because that is the main form of communication in the world.

Sipho: …hath not a homeless man hands, ……

V/O
Sipho knows what it’s like to be without a home, it’s only recently that he and his friend Gift have found a place to live behind a deserted house in Bertrams.

Sipho Nyhilia
Sipho I was in a very devastating state of mind stressed as how to get job I eventually joined in that’s where I got to test my few abilities as a person.

Link: Dorothy started Jam in 2012 with 7 men that she recruited from a soup kitchen. Many of them had been living on the streets since they were children. The lessons are free but when they do perform in public they get to keep their earnings.

V/O
Every Monday morning the group meets, and in between tea and sandwiches the men learn and perform renowned theatre works and it all started with the words of William Shakespeare.

Dorothy: I thought let’s start with powerful stories which the Shakespeare stories are let’s start with something that even a professional actor finds it hard to do.

Lwazi: We are such stuff as dreams are made of and our little life is rounded with a sleep.

Lwazi Mayeki
V/O
Lwazi was a homeless drug user when he joined Jam in 2012. He came from the Eastern Cape. For him Johannesburg was no City of Gold.

Lwazi: At first I thought I would end up on streets that my life is just finished I was meant to stay on the streets and do those things and maybe die on the streets so when Dorothy came through it was a breath of fresh air she gave me hope.

V/O
Shakespeare was the start, but the theatre group also performs other great works, including their own.

Innocent: We are the next big thing Yebo

V/O
Jam keeps going on a wing and a prayer. St George’s Church in Parktown and St Michael’s in Bryanston donate to the theatre group… otherwise it’s Dorothy and the kindness of friends.

Louis ……standing in front of an audience of different colours skin so that makes me, pull out of me the best of myself.

V/O
For Louis, the eldest member of the group, this is his family…and he has re-discovered his dream to write.

Louis T. Kalombo
Louis: I came as somebody who wants to learn so I was coming early putting chairs for other and then I was waiting for my opportunity so when the opportunity came I grab it with both hands. I say I am not going to let it go so that is how I started I can direct my own work and I am able to read other people things understand and direct it

V/O
The core members have had small parts in films, industrial theatre pieces and the hugely popular television soapie Generations. At a recent restaurant performance, each actor earned R 500.00

Up Sound Michael : To Be or Not to Be that is the question whether it is nobler in the mind to suffer the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune…

Michael Doctor Mazibuko
Claire: A lot of people say that Shakespeare was an English writer that lived 400 years ago are his stories still relevant today for a young black SA?
Michael : Of course they are still relevant of course
Michael: I am so very interested in Hamlet stories because it touches me. Sometimes if you think to Kill yourself you wont you will not commit suicide if you read that piece.

V/ O
And Michael has translated Shakespeare’s Sonnet 25 into isiZulu, which has helped him master English.

Michael: Firstly I didn’t know how to speak English it was very difficult on top of that I am here to learn Shakespeare it was quiet difficult … so she told me to translate this other sonnet 25 to Iszulu make sure you own English take English and own you know.

V/O
Last year Dorothy was awarded a Naledi - South Africa’s equivalent of the Toni’s - for this innovation in theatre.

Dorothy And can you imagine what it was like at the Naledi Awards last year where their were 1 800 people it is like being a soccer player or something.

V/O
Michael first job on television was on Generations and he envisions an even brighter future.

Michael: The first job that I got on TV was Generations..Law of Attraction I attracted that Job on Generations
Dorothy What is the next thing you are attracting
Michael: The next thing I am attracting is to get a SA SAFTA awards I want an award

Link: But it’s not all Sunshine and Roses Jam has experienced some setbacks , participants of the programme have either relapsed from drugs, have lost their lives due to illness or even been murdered

Claire: How does it feel that you could change your life with this programme and others couldn’t?
Lwazi: Yes but at the same time it is a motivation for me I don’t want to end up like they have ended up.
Claire: Where would you be if it weren’t for Jam?
LAUGHS I think I would just be another guy on the streets, seriously or maybe in a grave.

V/O
Teboho hustles on the streets of Parkhurst. He’s the group’s most recent recruit, and he has started writing and performing his own pieces

Teboho Mabuseloi
Tebohe: Day by day critics hits our skin hide way they say ……

V/O
While we were filming this insert, Teboho found a job.

Teboho: The group has given me confidence have given me realisation I am also important I am also a person that can make things happen for themselves.

V/O
Embarking on this journey, these men have discovered new territory in their own lives, their own place in this world.

Claire What do you want for your life now?
Lwazi :I would like to teach some other guys who are on the streets guys who are welcome from the Eastern Cape Whatever I got taught in this world I would like to impart to someone else to make a difference in some one else’s life …

V/O
And the rewards are multiplying.

Dorothy: if I say that working with them is the most important and joyous part of my life that’s the truth. I have learnt as much from them as they have learnt from me.

Dorothy: if I say that working with them is the most important and joyous part of my life that’s the truth. I have learnt as much from them as they have learnt from me.

metadata.Summary: In between taxis, and hawkers and piles of rubbish, squeezed in between decaying buildings, there’s a sign – easy to miss- that announces the Hillbrow Theatre…then down the stairs you go until to the basement and here amongst the broken chairs… England’s most famous playwright; William Shakespeare’s words are being given new life and meaning. Around 15 men of various ages are sitting in a semi- circle. Playing to this audience is 31 year old Michael Mazibuko. He’s reciting Hamlet’s soliloquy ‘ To Be or Not To Be’. Director, Michael Maxwell is giving Mazibuko voice direction and explaining the meanings of some of these very olde English words – while he is doing this you could hear a pin drop, everyone’s attention is focused on Michaels every word. Called Johannesburg Awakening ( Jam), this is brain child of Dorothy Anne Gould, one of South Africa’s most celebrated and respected actresses, Dorothy has starred in over 180 productions and been awarded several of South Africa’s top accolades. Dorothy’s own life was changed as teenager when she discovered the power of the spoken word. "I fell in love with the stories and poetry of a man called William Shakespeare. These made a profound shift in my immature consciousness to a more spiritual level of understanding of my world and of humanity; they made me aware that performance in a story is a sacred art and can transform both performer and audience and that this is achieved through the use of breath, through the power of the spoken word and through the act of sublimating ones ego and playing instead, for the gods. They gave me a purpose in my life which has never wavered – uplift and serve ones’ fellow human beings through the power and magic of poetry."
metadata.Further information: It was this she wanted to pass on and hopefully transform other lives. She started Jam in 2012 with seven men and one woman recruited from a church soup kitchen. Some had been on the streets since they were children. With weekly classes, teaching Shakespeare and poetry and classes in acting and voice the group has grown and many have managed to improve their lives and gain employment. They range in age from 18 – 56 years old. The classes have gradually seen men like Michael Mazibuko or Bongani Dlamini find their voice, their self respect and ambition. Dorothy “When you have never had a voice it takes time and courage to find it…... When your spoken voice is put out in the world then the power and images of the words start to flow through and that to some measure heals your pain.” Shakespeare was a tough place to start but Dorothy did it also for the shock tactic: ‘ If you can recite Hamlets soliloquy at the traffic lights you will probably get some money because people don’t expect that so its breaking assumptions. “The men challenge my assumptions too with their eloquence, enthusiasm and skills.” They meet every Monday… now not only learning but finding their own voice in prose or poetry telling their truth’s. Formerly homeless, Scott Edmn, has been with the group since the beginning, Scott makes the sandwiches and tea which are donated St Georges Church , and very welcome. Scott also keeps an order in the proceedings… Michael Mazibuko says he has found his soul in Hamlet’s To Be or Not to Be “it speaks directly to me about the challenges I face every day” It also helped him learn English when Mama D (as the call Dorothy) asked him to help her translate some pieces to iZulu; Last month he played a part in soapie ‘Generations’ and was paid. Some of the others have also played roles in films and soaps. Iwasi Mayeki, in rehearsal for Shakespeare’s Richard III, starts his soliloquy, when he reaches the line “ dogs bark at me as I halt by them,” you know he knows exactly what that feels like. Because Iwasi, has been homeless for most of his life. Shakespeare’s words relate directly to them and reflect their own circumstances says Myeki…he was one of the original crew and joined out of curiosity. Myeke was a homeless drug user and credits Jam for turning his life around. ‘I found a place where `I can talk and my voice can be heard. It gave me something to believe in. Now I am an actor and before I was just another kid on the streets. The stories Shakespeare tells are still relevant today because it’s not just about events. It’s about people and the human condition. It talks about love and tragedy and things that are happening in our lives. Some characters have lost everything so we can connect to what he writes about. We are the perfect people to tell his stories because we have been through a lot.’ Last year Dorothy was awarded a Naledi ( the South African equivalent of the Oscars)for this innovation in theatre. The group have grown to 20 and their determination under her guidance has helped many improve their circumstance. The lessons are free and when they perform in public they keep their earnings. Most now have roofs over their heads and one sponsor pays for three of them to share a flat in Hillbrow. This is my home, 29 year old Bongani Dlamini’s says and with a touch of drama he adds, it kept him alive. ‘ If it wasn’t for Shakespeare I wouldn’t have even gone to rehab. I was giving up because I had nothing to do and no money, I was using being an orphan as an excuse and having a lot of resentment. I always had a lot of excuses’ Shakespeare’s characters give him hope and strength because the tribulations they are experiencing are nothing new ‘ . But its not all rainbow’s and roses Jam has seen setbacks and sadness. too with one actor going back to drugs after appearing in adverts and one relapsing after earning a place in a drama school. Four have died - two murdered one from a drug related heart attack and one from pneumonia. One was Charles who died after writing a beautiful piece saying ‘ Now I can hold up my head high’ On the 14th April the group will perform in Melville which would be good to film as part of the story… To tell the actors story through their interviews, in their words that are now being listened to. What Dorothy has done is what she knows how to do and the creative process touches and transforms both the actor and the director Teaching Shakespeare at our South African schools has come under some controversy, but during freedom fighter, Sonny Venkatrathnam’s, incarceration on Robben Island, he smuggled in a copy of ‘The Complete Works of William Shakespeare’ disguised as a bible. This was passed between a number of prisoners including Nelson Mandela…Mandela’s signature was found next to a quote from Julius Caesar ‘ Cowards die many times before their deaths , the valiant never taste death but once’. In April and May the 9th Shakespeare schools Festival kicks off and it will be dedicated to Sonny Venkatrathnam.
